# Laws of war (humanitarian law) (`laws_of_war`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by international_law_sovereignty, golden_rule_universal_ethics, human_equality_dignity, written_law_code
- Core idea: Rules of war developed in different legal and religious traditions. In modern humanitarian law civilians are protected against direct attack unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities. Combatants who surrender, or who are incapacitated by wounds and refrain from hostile acts and escape, are also protected. Wounded people must receive care, and prisoners must be treated humanely. These obligations apply even when the other side violates them. In earlier periods customs concerning surrender, treatment of captives and protected messengers varied. Later treaties, military instruction, prisoner records and independent relief organisations gave these protections institutional form.
- Pitfalls:
  - Rules that protect only one's own kind (fellow Greeks, Christians, Muslims) leave everyone else outside
  - Whether a war is just and how it is fought are separate questions; a just cause does not license atrocity
  - Assuming an enemy violation permits retaliation against prisoners or other protected people
  - Until the 19th century custom allowed a town that refused surrender and was stormed to be sacked, which every besieged garrison (Vienna 1683) had to weigh
  - Assuming the Geneva Conventions were the first such rules; codes exist in ancient India, China, Greece and early Islam
- History: india: c. 2nd c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Laws of Manu 7.90–93 forbid poisoned and concealed weapons and killing those who surrender, sleep or are disarmed; china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – Sun Tzu advises treating captives well; Zuozhuan records rules of honourable combat; greece: 5th c. BC – inviolable heralds, truces to recover the dead, sacred sites spared (often broken); rome: by 3rd c. BC – fetial procedure for declaring a just war; 44 BC – Cicero, De officiis I.34–40; islamic: 632 – Abu Bakr's instructions to spare women, children, the old, monks and fruit trees; c. 800 – al-Shaybani's treatise on the law of nations (siyar); europe: 5th–13th c. – just war doctrine of Augustine and Aquinas; 1625 – Grotius; 1864 – first Geneva Convention after Dunant's account of Solferino; 1899 and 1907 – Hague Regulations; 1929 – prisoner of war convention; 1945–1946 – Nuremberg trials; americas: 1863 – Lieber Code for the Union armies; global: 1949 – four Geneva Conventions
- Read:
  - Hugo Grotius, De jure belli ac pacis (1625)
  - Henry Dunant, Un souvenir de Solférino (1862)
  - Geoffrey Best, Humanity in Warfare (1980)
